title: How to Reverse Engineer a Job Description with AI
description: You have found the perfect job listing. The title matches your experience, the company culture sounds right, and the location is convenient. But when you read the requirements, you feel a pang of doubt. Do you actually have the specific tools listed? Do you have the exact number of years of experience they demand? It is easy to feel like you do not fit the mold, even if you are highly qualified. The problem is that job descriptions are often written by HR departments, not the people who will actually do the work. They are checklists, not blueprints. If you apply with a generic resume, you are competing against hundreds of others doing the same thing. The solution is to stop reading the description passively and start analyzing it actively. By using AI tools to break down the language, you can identify the true priorities of the role and tailor your application to speak directly to the hiring manager's needs. Key takeaways Use AI to separate 'nice-to-have' skills from 'must-have' core competencies. Identify the underlying problem the role is meant to solve, not just the tasks. Tailor your resume bullet points to mirror the specific language of the job spec. Verify technical requirements against your actual experience to avoid false positives. Extracting the Core Problem Statement Most job descriptions list tasks, but they rarely explain the business outcome those tasks achieve. A 'Content Writer' role might list 'write blog posts,' but the core problem might be 'increase organic traffic by 20%.' To find this, you need to look past the bullet points. The first step in reverse engineering is to ask an AI assistant to synthesize the entire text into a single, clear objective. This helps you understand the strategic value of the position. When you understand the core problem, you can frame your experience in terms of results rather than duties. Instead of saying 'I managed social media accounts,' you can say 'I drove engagement growth by implementing a consistent posting strategy.' This shift in perspective is crucial for standing out. It shows you are thinking like a partner, not just an employee. Copy the entire job description text. Paste it into ChatGPT or Claude with the prompt: 'Summarize the primary business problem this role is hired to solve in one sentence.' Ask the AI to list the top three key outcomes the hiring manager expects from this position within the first 90 days. Compare these outcomes with your past achievements to find the strongest matches. Pro tip: If the AI identifies a vague objective, ask it to clarify based on industry standards for that specific job title. chatgpt claude Decoding Skill Priorities and Keywords Job descriptions are dense with keywords, but not all keywords are created equal. Some are essential technical requirements, while others are soft skills or general expectations. Applicants often fail because they miss the subtle emphasis on certain tools or methodologies. For example, a marketing role might list 'SEO' and 'Content Strategy,' but the context might reveal that technical SEO is the primary driver of success, not just content volume. You can use AI to categorize these skills. Ask the model to separate the requirements into 'Must-Have' and 'Nice-to-Have' categories based on the frequency and context of their mention. This helps you decide where to focus your resume. If a skill is listed in the first paragraph or repeated multiple times, it is likely a deal-breaker if missing. If it appears only in a long list of secondary duties, it may be less critical. Ask the AI to extract all hard skills and soft skills mentioned in the description. Instruct the AI to rank these skills by importance based on their placement and repetition in the text. Identify any specific software or tools mentioned and note their context (e.g., 'expert level' vs. 'familiar with'). Cross-reference this list with your own skill set to identify gaps. Pro tip: Pay close attention to the first three requirements listed; these are often the non-negotiables. gemini Analyzing Company Culture and Tone The tone of a job description is a strong indicator of the company’s culture. Is it formal and structured, or casual and innovative? Does it emphasize individual achievement or team collaboration? Understanding this cultural fit is just as important as matching technical skills. A mismatch in tone can lead to a poor interview experience, even if your resume is perfect. The words used in the description provide clues about the daily work environment and the values the company holds dear. You can ask an AI to analyze the language patterns in the description. Look for words like 'fast-paced,' 'autonomous,' 'collaborative,' or 'data-driven.' These adjectives paint a picture of how the team operates. If the description uses 'we' frequently, it suggests a collaborative culture. If it uses 'you' or 'individual,' it may indicate a more independent role. Aligning your cover letter and interview answers with this cultural insight can significantly boost your chances of success. Ask the AI to identify the top five cultural values implied by the job description. Request a summary of the communication style (formal, casual, aggressive, supportive). Note any phrases that indicate work-life balance expectations or remote work flexibility. Draft a brief paragraph for your cover letter that reflects these cultural insights. Pro tip: Mirror the language of the job description in your cover letter to show alignment with company values. perplexity Tailoring Your Resume with AI Assistance Once you have a clear understanding of the role’s priorities, you can tailor your resume to match. This does not mean lying or exaggerating your experience. It means highlighting the most relevant parts of your background. If the job description emphasizes 'stakeholder management,' ensure your resume includes specific examples of how you managed stakeholders. If it highlights 'Python scripting,' make sure your technical skills section lists Python prominently. You can use AI to help rewrite your bullet points. Paste your current resume bullet points and the job description into an AI tool. Ask it to suggest how to rephrase your achievements to align with the job’s specific language and priorities. This process helps you present your experience in the most compelling way possible. It ensures that the keywords from the job description are naturally integrated into your resume, helping you pass through Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) and catch the eye of human reviewers. Paste your current resume and the job description into an AI tool. Ask the AI to identify which of your current bullet points are most relevant to the job. Request suggestions for rephrasing those bullet points to include specific keywords from the job description. Review the suggestions and manually edit them to ensure they remain accurate and authentic. Pro tip: Always verify that the AI’s suggested rephrasings accurately reflect your actual experience before using them. grammarly Preparing for Interview Questions Reverse engineering a job description also helps you prepare for the interview. By understanding the core problems and key skills, you can anticipate the questions the interviewer will ask. For example, if the role emphasizes 'problem-solving,' expect behavioral questions about times you solved complex issues. If it emphasizes 'teamwork,' expect questions about how you collaborate with others. This preparation allows you to craft specific, relevant examples that demonstrate your fit for the role. You can use AI to generate potential interview questions based on the job description. Ask the model to create a list of ten likely questions, categorized by topic (e.g., technical, behavioral, situational). Then, use the same tool to help you draft your answers. This practice helps you refine your messaging and ensures you are ready to speak confidently about your experience. It also helps you identify any gaps in your knowledge or experience that you may need to address during the interview. Ask the AI to generate 10 likely interview questions based on the job description. Categorize the questions by type (technical, behavioral, cultural fit). Draft answers for the most critical questions, using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Review your answers to ensure they are concise and directly address the job’s key requirements. Pro tip: Practice answering these questions out loud to improve your delivery and confidence. Evaluating the Fit and Making a Decision Finally, use the insights you have gathered to evaluate whether the role is truly a good fit for you. Reverse engineering a job description is not just about getting the job; it is about ensuring the job is right for you. If the core problem does not align with your career goals, or if the cultural tone does not match your working style, it may be worth reconsidering. This objective analysis helps you make a more informed decision about whether to apply or move on to the next opportunity. Consider the long-term implications of the role. Does it offer the growth opportunities you are looking for? Does it align with your values and lifestyle? The AI analysis can help you see the role from a different perspective, providing a clearer picture of what to expect. This holistic approach ensures that you are not just chasing a job title, but investing in a career path that brings you satisfaction and success. List your top three career goals and values. Compare these goals with the core problem and cultural insights from the job description. Identify any significant mismatches or red flags. Make a final decision on whether to apply, based on the overall fit. Pro tip: If there are mismatches, consider whether they are deal-breakers or areas you can grow into. notion AI Tools for Job Description Analysis | Tool | Best For | Key Feature | |---|---|---| | ChatGPT | General analysis and drafting | Versatile language processing | | Claude | Detailed cultural and tone analysis | Nuanced understanding of context | | Perplexity | Researching company context | Web search integration | | Grammarly | Polishing resume language | Real-time grammar and style checks | FAQ Can AI replace my human judgment in applying for jobs? No. AI is a tool to help you analyze and tailor your application, but it cannot replace your authentic experience or human judgment. Always review and edit AI-generated content to ensure it accurately reflects your skills and values. How do I handle job descriptions that are vague or poorly written? If a job description is vague, use AI to ask clarifying questions based on industry standards. You can also research the company’s other job postings or recent news to gain more context about their priorities and culture. Is it okay to use AI to rewrite my resume? Yes, as long as you maintain honesty. Use AI to improve clarity, impact, and keyword alignment, but never invent experience or exaggerate your achievements. The goal is to present your true self in the best possible light. How long does it take to reverse engineer a job description? It typically takes 15-30 minutes for a standard job description. This includes extracting key insights, tailoring your resume, and preparing for potential interview questions. The time investment is well worth the improved quality of your application. Bottom line Reverse engineering a job description with AI transforms the application process from a passive guesswork exercise into a strategic analysis. By identifying the core problems, prioritizing skills, and aligning with company culture, you can present yourself as a much stronger candidate. This method saves time and increases your chances of landing interviews with roles that are truly a good fit. Start by breaking down your next target job description with an AI assistant to see the difference. Originally published at https://blog.atlasasistent.com/how-to-reverse-engineer-a-job-description-with-ai. More free tools: https://blog.atlasasistent.com/tools

title: I deleted plan.md. My AI agent now plans, logs and proves its work in one file.
description: Most AI coding setups keep two documents: a plan the agent writes once, and notes/memory it forgets to update. By Tuesday the plan describes a project that no longer exists. I had a progress log and was about to add a plan file next to it. Then I asked the obvious question: do these two need to be separate files? They didn't. Here is what I changed and where you can take it. What I started with My brief was short: keep a log of which subtasks are done, tell me when to compact, and tell the compactor what to throw away. In my words: make sure that it reminds to compact? so that it is not losing context for the next set of tasks and saving on the credits. That became the progress-log skill for Claude Code. A hook reminds the agent to compact between groups of work, gives the compactor rules on what to keep and what to drop, and restores the log afterwards. A fresh context no longer means a fresh start. None of this is a new idea. Anthropic's guide to context engineering names both halves: compaction, which summarises a conversation near the context limit and starts a new window from the summary, and structured note-taking, where the agent "regularly writes notes persisted to memory outside of the context window" [1]. Keeping the window small matters too: Chroma's context rot study found that model performance "grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows" [2]. The skill is my attempt to make those two habits automatic. Why plan.md was the wrong second file A plan and a log answer different questions. The plan says what we are doing and why. The log says where we are now. The plan changes rarely; the log changes after every subtask. That sounds like a reason to keep them apart. In practice, three things went wrong: Compaction. After a compact, the hook restores the end of progress.md. A separate plan.md would not come back on its own. Visibility. The timeline pane reads one file. A plan outside it never shows. Drift. With two files, the plan says one thing while the log has moved on, and nothing notices. So the plan moved into the log, and the agent is told never to create a plan.md at all. Each task section now carries its goal, its groups of subtasks, and its proof: ## Add login (2026-11-06) Goal: users can sign in with Google. Done means a new user reaches the dashboard. ### OAuth - [x] Callback route, 6 tests pass - [ ] (background) Run the full test suite ### Sessions - [ ] Session expiry Notes: chose cookies over JWT because we need server-side logout. | Goal | Evidence | Achieved | |---|---|---| | New user reaches dashboard | e2e test passes | Yes | The rule that makes it work: a box is ticked only when a test, a command result or a PR shows the work is done. "Done" without evidence stays unticked. Labels such as (background) and (subagent) say how each subtask runs, so the plan doubles as a work order. Here is the loop the hooks run around that file. Claude Code fires a PreCompact hook before compaction and a SessionStart hook whose matcher includes compact when the session resumes after one [3]: It's ReAct, written down The loop isn't new either. In 2022, ReAct showed that language models do better when they "generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner" [5] Think, act, look at the result, think again. Claude Code's agent already works this way. What progress.md adds is a place for that loop to live outside the context window: ReAct step In progress.md Thought The goal, the groups and the next unticked box Action The agent works that subtask Observation The evidence: a test result, a command output, a PR In ReAct the trace sits in the model's context, so in a long session it gets summarised away at the next compaction. Here it's written to a file and survives. The evidence column is the observation step you can audit. The pane A log nobody reads is a diary. I wanted it in front of me while I work, so I built progress-timeline, a Claude Code mod that shows the log as a timeline in a pane beside the chat. Green is done, yellow is in progress, grey is planned. It opens by itself when a new plan appears. My review of the first working version, verbatim: this looks awesome? thankyou!!!! Engineering standards remain high. Get it The repository: how-saket-claudes The skill: progress-log The pane: progress-timeline Install the pane from the repository's plugin marketplace. In Claude Code, a marketplace is "a catalog that lists plugins and where to fetch each one" [4]: claude plugin install progress-timeline --marketplace iaintsaket/how-saket-claudes The skill's compaction reminders need Claude Code hooks and Python 3. Setup steps are in hooks-setup.md in the repository. Before you copy this It is a convention, not magic. The pane only reads the format above, so any tool or person can write the file. The agent still makes mistakes. The evidence column exists so you can check its claims instead of trusting them. The pane needs room. Claude Code only opens it unasked in a wide terminal. In a narrow one, run /progress-timeline to open it yourself. It docks on the right, and that can't be changed. If you try it, tell me what broke for you. References Anthropic Applied AI team, Effective context engineering for AI agents, 29 September 2025. Kelly Hong, Anton Troynikov and Jeff Huber, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance, Chroma technical report, 14 July 2025. Claude Code documentation, Hooks reference. Claude Code documentation, Plugins overview. Shunyu Yao, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan and Yuan Cao, ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, arXiv:2210.03629, 6 October 2022.
